title: Corniche
description: A poem from Les Murray's Subhuman Redneck Poems (1996) in which the fear of dying turns into a longing for death as the only cure; one of the bleakest poems of his late middle age.
plot_or_argument: 'Corniche' belongs to the group of poems in Subhuman Redneck Poems that Murray wrote out of depression, and its movement is the reverse of the elegy's: instead of mourning a death, it finds in the thought of death a kind of peace. The speaker, awake in the hours before dawn, follows the fear to its end and discovers that the fear has become a wish, and the poem's short lines and plain diction keep the argument from becoming a consolation. The title names a coast road, the kind of road that runs along a cliff edge, and the poem's position is that of someone driving between the sea and the drop. The poem is not a suicide note but an honest record of a state of mind, and Murray's later work returned to the subject of depression with the same refusal of comfort.
narrative_structure: A short poem in brief lines, with little narrative and a single turn from fear to longing; its form is the argument's movement, and the title provides the landscape the poem does not otherwise describe.
meter_and_prosody: Plain, short-breathed lines with no ornament; the diction is ordinary and the tone level, so that the reversal arrives without rhetorical preparation; the poem's power is in what it withholds.
historical_context: Subhuman Redneck Poems (Duffy and Snellgrove, 1996) won the T. S. Eliot Prize and is Murray's darkest collection, written in the period of his severe depression; 'Corniche' is one of the poems critics single out as among the most difficult and most honest in it.
literary_significance: A key poem of Murray's darkest collection and a standard example of his late manner; it is his second selection in the Norton Anthology, and its treatment of depression is among the most discussed in his work.
bibliographical_notes: Published in Subhuman Redneck Poems (Sydney: Duffy and Snellgrove, 1996) and collected in Collected Poems (2018). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 966.
thematic_analysis: The poem's subject is the mutability of feeling: the fear of death that drives the speaker becomes, by the end of the poem, a longing for it, and the poem traces that reversal without judging it. Depression is described from inside, as a condition in which the worst thing and the only cure are the same, and the poem's brevity keeps the reader in that moment rather than resolving it into either consolation or despair.
summary: A short poem set in the pre-dawn hours, in which the speaker's dread of death becomes a desire for it, and the poem's argument turns on the discovery that the thing feared is also the only release.
research_notes: The collection and the poem's subject are established from Peter Goldsworthy's review of Collected Poems, which discusses 'Corniche' and the pre-dawn poems of Subhuman Redneck Poems; the text was not read complete, so the record makes no quotation.

title: The Drowned World
description: J. G. Ballard's second novel (1962), in which solar radiation has melted the polar ice caps and turned London into a tropical lagoon, and a biologist, Robert Kerans, chooses the drowned world and its Triassic pull over the work of restoring the old one.
plot_or_argument: The novel is set in a future, some decades after solar radiation has melted the ice caps and raised the seas, when the drowned cities of Europe have become lagoons and reefs. Robert Kerans, a biologist, is part of a small expedition surveying the drowned London; the heat is rising year by year, and the survivors live in the upper floors of the great buildings, diving into the submerged streets and hunting the giant reptiles and iguanas that have colonised the lagoon. Kerans, his colleague Bodkin and the soldier Riggs are joined by Beatrice Dahl, a wealthy and detached woman whose apartment on the water is the novel's centre of what remains of civilised life, and by Strangman, the leader of a gang of scavengers who drains the lagoon around the city to loot it. As the temperature climbs, Kerans begins to dream of the drowned world and to feel the pull of the Triassic past, and Bodkin, an older scientist who has studied the fossils of the sun, walks south into the jungle and is not seen again. When Strangman's men drain the lagoon and expose the city, Kerans sees the drowned world he loved destroyed, and after the water returns he refuses the expedition's plan to evacuate north and sets out southward after Bodkin, towards the sun, the reptiles and the lost evolutionary age. The novel ends with Kerans alone in the jungle, having chosen regression rather than recovery, and with the question of whether he is mad or has understood something the others cannot.
narrative_structure: A short novel in three parts, set almost entirely in the drowned London and its lagoon; the plot is a sequence of encounters and discoveries rather than a quest, and the final movement is westward and southward, away from the expedition's route home; the ending refuses the rescue that the earlier chapters seem to promise.
meter_and_prosody: A cool, exact, descriptive prose, with the temperature and the light registered on every page; the imagery of drained swimming pools, submerged office blocks, giant reptiles and stagnant water; little dialogue and almost no interior monologue of the conventional kind; the science is delivered as observation rather than explanation.
historical_context: The Drowned World appeared in shortened form in Science Fiction Adventures in January 1962 and in book form from Victor Gollancz in 1962; it belongs with The Drought (1965) and The Crystal World (1966) to the 'ambiguous apocalypse' sequence of Ballard's early novels and to the New Wave of British science fiction, and it has since been read as a foundational text of climate fiction.
literary_significance: The novel that established Ballard's reputation and the first of his catastrophe books; it is his selection in the Norton Anthology (printed as the extract 'The Causeways of the Sun'), and the record covers the whole novel. It is now read as a founding text of climate fiction as well as a key novel of the New Wave, and it gave the word 'Ballardian' its first clear reference.
bibliographical_notes: First published in shortened form in Science Fiction Adventures (January 1962) and in book form by Victor Gollancz (London, 1962), with an American edition from Berkley Medallion. Norton prints an extract beginning on page 984; this record covers the whole novel.
thematic_analysis: The novel's central idea is that the catastrophe is not a disaster to be survived but a transformation to be accepted: the flood has returned the earth to its prehistoric state, and Kerans's dreams are the human mind responding to the same evolutionary pull. Ballard's 'inner space' is already at work here, since the drowned city is less a setting than a projection of the psyche, and the novel's refusal of the conventional adventure plot - there is no rescue, no rebuilding of civilisation - is its argument. The sun and the lagoon are narcotic, and the novel is ambivalent about them: the regression is both a liberation from the old social order and a surrender of everything that made Kerans a person. Read now, the book is also an early climate-fiction fable, in which the earth's warming is not reversed.
summary: A novel in which a small scientific team, marooned in the flooded ruins of London, tries to salvage what it can while the biologist Robert Kerans finds himself drawn by the heat, the reptiles and the triassic jungle that has replaced the city towards a regression into deep evolutionary time.
critical_context: The Drowned World was praised at once by Kingsley Amis and Michael Moorcock for its imaginative power and literary ambition, and it has since become the founding text of the reading of Ballard as a writer of 'inner space' rather than of gadgetry; critics group it with The Drought and The Crystal World as 'ambiguous apocalypse' novels that reject the recovery plot, and later criticism has treated it as an important early work of climate fiction. Its place in the Norton Anthology, as the Ballard selection, has consolidated its standing as the most literary of his early books.
research_notes: The plot and the novel's critical placing follow Wikipedia's article on the book, which was read directly; the account of Kerans's decision and the ending follows that summary, and the text itself was not read complete.

title: Looking for a Rain God
description: A story from Bessie Head's The Collector of Treasures (1977): during a seven-year drought in Botswana, a family sacrifices two young girls to the rain god, the rain does not come, and the crime is found out.
plot_or_argument: The story opens with the drought: the rains have failed for seven years, the harvests have been lost, and some of the villagers have hanged themselves rather than face the hunger. Mokgobja, an old man, and his son Ramadi take their family to plough a patch of land when a little rain comes, but the rain lasts only a fortnight and the women of the family begin to weep at night at the prospect of starvation. Mokgobja remembers an ancient ceremony, a sacrifice to the rain god, and he and Ramadi agree to it, taking the two little girls, Neo and Boseyong, out into the land and killing them. The rain does not come. The family returns to the village and the absence of the children is noticed; the police investigate, and Tiro, the girls' mother, breaks down and tells what happened. The story ends with Mokgobja and Ramadi sentenced to death for ritual murder, and with the narrator's flat statement that the family's hope of rain had been met by nothing. Head's method is to tell the story without sensationalism, so that the horror lies in the ordinariness of the decision and in the drought that made it conceivable.
narrative_structure: A single continuous narrative, moving from the general description of the drought to the family's hopes, the sacrifice, the failure of the rain and the discovery; the point of view is close to the community rather than to any one character, and the ending delivers the legal consequence in a single flat sentence.
meter_and_prosody: A plain, measured, almost biblical prose, with short declarative sentences and little metaphor; the narrative voice is that of a storyteller close to the village, using its idiom and its proverbs; the horror is conveyed by understatement and by the absence of commentary.
historical_context: The Collector of Treasures and Other Botswana Village Tales (Heinemann, 1977) was written in Serowe, where Head lived from 1964, and draws on the oral history she had collected for Serowe: Village of the Rain Wind; the story's drought and ritual belong to the remembered life of rural Botswana, and it was published in the Heinemann African Writers Series.
literary_significance: The best-known of Head's Botswana stories and one of the most widely taught African short stories in English; it is her selection in the Norton Anthology.
bibliographical_notes: Published in The Collector of Treasures and Other Botswana Village Tales (London: Heinemann, 1977). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 992.
thematic_analysis: The story examines what extreme scarcity does to belief: the rain-making sacrifice is not presented as exotic superstition but as the last resource of people who have nothing else, and the old man's faith is shown to be as rational, in its own terms, as the women's weeping. Head refuses to make the family monstrous, and the story's judgement falls on the drought, on the poverty that leaves no alternative, and on the collision between an inherited ritual and the law that will punish it. The girls themselves are barely present, and their absence is the story's moral centre.
summary: A spare narrative of a village in drought, of Mokgobja and his son Ramadi's decision to perform an old rain-making sacrifice with Ramadi's two daughters, and of the discovery and punishment that follow.
research_notes: The plot follows the study notes read as a search extract, which agree with general knowledge on the drought, the sacrifice of Neo and Boseyong and the death sentences; the names and the ending were checked there, and the text was not read complete.

title: What the Tapster Saw
description: The last story in Ben Okri's Stars of the New Curfew (1988): a palm-wine tapper falls from his tree and, in a week-long coma, sees the corruption, the oil wells and the violence of his country in a vision.
plot_or_argument: The story begins in confusion - 'I had died. Not even I' - and follows the tapster's spirit as it leaves his body after a fall from a palm tree he has climbed every day for thirty years. In the vision the land is being destroyed by the oil companies: forests are cut down and blown up, the earth is opened and left with oil and animal bones spewing out of it, bridges and roads are ruined by unexploded bombs from an old war, travellers are killed, and people the tapster knows are executed by bullets 'with their names on them'. A rainbow-coloured snake swims in a river and makes it clear and luminous; voices speak around him and beat him when he answers, giving him thoughts to replace the ones they have knocked out of him, such as 'the bigger mouth eats the smaller head'. Three turtles, one of them with the face of his herbalist friend, discuss the number of moons and stars with complete authority and complete ignorance. He meets a man who died reading the Bible upside down and recognises himself. At the end he wakes in his friend's house, where two turtles stand in a shrine in the corner, and he is left carrying a knowledge he cannot express.
narrative_structure: A first-person narrative in a single continuous vision, with no chapter divisions and a dream logic that moves between scenes without transition; the frame is the fall and the waking, and the vision's material is organised by recurrence (the snake, the turtles, the voices) rather than by plot.
meter_and_prosody: A dense, incantatory prose with the rhythms of oral narration; short sentences, repetition and catalogue; vivid, surreal imagery (the 'roseate' snake, the luminous river, the upside-down Bible); proverbs and aphorisms embedded in the narration; the first person is that of an uneducated man whose diction is nonetheless lyrical.
historical_context: Stars of the New Curfew (Secker and Warburg, 1988) gathers stories of Lagos and the oil-producing Delta written in the 1980s, the decade of the Nigerian oil boom's collapse; 'What the Tapster Saw' draws on Amos Tutuola's The Palm-Wine Drinkard (1952) and has been read by critics as an early example of 'petro-magic realism', the meeting of magical realism and the oil economy.
literary_significance: The best known of Okri's short stories and a standard example of African magical realism; it is his selection in the Norton Anthology and the story through which his early fiction is usually introduced.
bibliographical_notes: Published in Stars of the New Curfew (London: Secker and Warburg, 1988). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 996.
thematic_analysis: The story is a satire of the Nigerian oil economy written as a dream vision: the oil companies, the government and the voices that beat the tapster all belong to a system that destroys the land and punishes anyone who questions it, and the turtles' ignorant authority is the story's image of power without knowledge. Okri's method is to give the poor man's vision the authority of revelation, so that the reader sees what the tapster sees without the mediation of reportage, and the ending's silence - a truth that cannot be spoken - is itself a political statement about who is permitted to speak.
summary: A first-person narrative in which the tapster, having fallen from a palm tree, drifts between this world and the next, witnessing oil companies destroying the forest, voices that beat him when he speaks, a rainbow snake in a river, and three turtles who talk with the authority of the powerful.
research_notes: The plot follows the two Scalar project pages on the story read as search extracts, which quote its opening and describe the vision in detail and agree with each other; the text itself was not read complete, and the quotations are those printed in those pages.

title: The God of Small Things
description: Arundhati Roy's first novel (1997), the story of twins Estha and Rahel in Ayemenem, Kerala, and of the 'love laws' that punish the affair between their mother Ammu and the untouchable Velutha, told out of chronological order and moving towards its catastrophe.
plot_or_argument: The novel is set mostly in Ayemenem, in Kerala, in two times: the present, when Rahel returns as an adult to the family house and finds her twin Estha silent and damaged, and 1969, when the two were seven years old. Their mother Ammu, divorced and living with her children in her parents' house, falls in love with Velutha, an untouchable carpenter and communist, and the affair is discovered by the family: Ammu's brother Chacko, her aunt Baby Kochamma, and the police, who beat Velutha nearly to death and blame him for the drowning of Sophie Mol, the English cousin who had come to stay with her mother Margaret and who dies in the river during the children's attempt to run away. The twins are separated after the crisis, Estha is sent to his father and stops speaking, Ammu dies alone in a hotel, and Rahel drifts through an unhappy marriage. The novel's narration circles these events, moving backwards and forwards between the 1960s, the 1970s and the 1990s and between the children's perceptions and the adult narrator's retelling, so that the catastrophe is known from the first pages and its causes are assembled gradually. The title is taken from a line about the 'God of Loss' and the 'God of Small Things', and the novel's subject is the way the small, ordinary details of a childhood carry the whole of a life.
narrative_structure: A non-linear narration in twenty-one chapters, moving between 1969, the 1970s and the 1990s, and between the twins' childhood perspective and an adult retrospective voice; information is withheld and revealed out of order, and the novel's central events are shown twice, from different points in time.
meter_and_prosody: A prose of great syntactic invention, with word-play, portmanteau compounds and capitalised phrases that render the children's speech ('Being made to stand outside the door', 'the Orangedrink Lemondrink Man'); a lyricism that is precise about the material world (pickles, bananas, boats, the river) and ironic about the adult one; dialogue in a Kerala English with Malayalam cadences.
historical_context: The God of Small Things was published by IndiaInk and Penguin in 1997 and won the Booker Prize in the same year; it drew on Roy's childhood in Ayemenem and on her mother's family, and its publication was a landmark in the international reception of Indian writing in English. Roy's subsequent career as a political essayist has shaped the reading of the novel's politics ever since.
literary_significance: The most celebrated Indian novel in English of the 1990s and the first by an Indian woman to win the Booker Prize; it is Roy's selection in the Norton Anthology, printed as the extract 'God's Own Country', and the record covers the whole novel. Its opening sentence and its children's-eye narration are among the most widely quoted in postcolonial fiction in English.
bibliographical_notes: Published in 1997 by IndiaInk (New Delhi) and Penguin Books (London). Norton prints an extract under the title 'God's Own Country', beginning on page 1002; this record covers the whole novel.
thematic_analysis: The novel's central subject is the 'love laws' that decide 'who should be loved, and how, and how much': the caste and class order of Kerala forbids Ammu's love for Velutha, and the family enforces it with a cruelty that is both social and personal. The twins' bond is the counter-law, a love that survives separation and damage, and the novel's method - the child's-eye view, the withheld chronology - makes the reader experience the adult world as the children did, as a series of incomprehensible prohibitions that turn violent. History is present throughout: communism in Kerala, the Syrian Christian community, the memory of colonialism, and the post-independence order in which the police can destroy an untouchable man without consequence.
summary: A novel in which the twins, separated as children and reunited as adults, remember the events of 1969 - the visit of their English cousin Sophie Mol, the death by drowning that followed, and the police destruction of Velutha - and the family's history across three generations in Kerala.
critical_context: The novel's reception has been divided between admiration for its language and structure and suspicion of its commercial success: critics have praised the child's-eye narration and the treatment of caste, and have debated whether its lyricism aestheticises the violence it describes. Roy's later political writing has made the novel's politics a continuing subject, and its place in the syllabus of postcolonial fiction is secure; The Ministry of Utmost Happiness (2017) was read against it as a return to fiction after twenty years of essays.
research_notes: The plot follows Wikipedia's article on Roy and general knowledge of the novel, whose chronology and catastrophe are widely summarised; the text was not read complete in this session, so the record's quotations are limited to the phrase 'love laws', which is the novel's own term, and to the reported title of the extract found in the Norton list.

title: Death by Landscape
description: A story from Atwood's Wilderness Tips (1991): Lois, widowed and living in Toronto, looks at her collection of Canadian landscape paintings and remembers the summer at Camp Manitou when her friend Lucy disappeared from a cliff above the lake.
plot_or_argument: Lois, now widowed and living alone in a Toronto condominium overlooking Lake Ontario, has filled her walls with Canadian landscape paintings - 'every one of them is a picture of Lucy', as the story's last line puts it. The story moves back to her summers at Camp Manitou, a girls' camp in the northern Ontario bush, where she was sent from the age of nine and where she became friends with Lucy, a girl from Chicago whose parents were divorcing and who was, by their last summer, moody and restless. On a canoe trip into the interior the two girls climb a trail to a lookout above the lake; Lucy steps off the path to relieve herself and does not come back. Lois hears a scream - or thinks she hears one - and raises the alarm, but no trace of Lucy is ever found. The camp director's insinuation that Lois may have pushed her, the police search, and the return to a camp where the girls' bunk is rearranged so that no one has to sleep in Lucy's bed are the story's aftermath. In the present, Lois has spent her life living 'two lives', she says, one of them the life in which Lucy went on existing somewhere in the landscape; and the paintings, which she has bought without quite knowing why, become the place where the lost girl is kept.
narrative_structure: A double narrative, moving without chapter breaks between the present of Lois's apartment and the remembered summers at Camp Manitou; the story is told in close third person, in the iterative present for the camp years and in a slower present for Lois's old age, and ends on a short declarative sentence that reverses the meaning of everything before it.
meter_and_prosody: A cool, exact, deceptively flat prose with a journalist's eye for period detail (the camp songs, the wartime rationing, the girls' nicknames) and a poet's ear for the sentence as a unit of disclosure; the paintings are described in the language of art criticism, and the wilderness in the language of the camp brochure, so that neither is allowed to be innocent.
historical_context: Wilderness Tips (McClelland and Stewart, 1991) gathers stories written in the late 1980s, several of them, like this one, about women revisiting the myths of Canadian childhood; the camp story belongs to the tradition of Canadian writing about the bush that runs from Susanna Moodie through Atwood's own Survival (1972) and her Moodie poems in The Journals of Susanna Moodie (1970).
literary_significance: One of Atwood's most anthologised stories and a standard text in courses on Canadian literature, on the short story and on ecocriticism; it is her selection in the Norton Anthology alongside the poem 'Miss July Grows Older'.
bibliographical_notes: Published in Wilderness Tips (Toronto: McClelland and Stewart, 1991; London: Bloomsbury, 1991). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 1031. The Norton list does not print a date for it; it is dated here to the collection.
thematic_analysis: The story is about the wilderness as an idea rather than a place: the camp domesticates it with songs, canoes and schedules, while the real bush beyond the portages is indifferent and bottomless, and Lucy's disappearance is the point at which the two meet. Atwood uses the Canadian landscape tradition - the Group of Seven paintings Lois collects - as a critique: the paintings turn the wilderness into property and scenery, and yet they are also the only place where Lois can put her grief. Guilt, memory and the unreliability of witness run through the story, which never settles whether Lucy fell, was taken, or chose to vanish.
summary: A story in two times: the elderly Lois in her waterfront apartment among her Group of Seven landscapes, and the thirteen-year-old Lois at a girls' summer camp in northern Ontario, where a canoe trip ends with her friend's disappearance and a lifetime of unexplained guilt.
research_notes: The plot follows the EBSCO Research Starters entry on the story, read as a search extract, which agrees with other summaries on the camp, the cliff, the scream and the paintings; the text itself was not read complete, and the quotations are those printed in that entry and in the critical article cited for the poem.

title: Miss July Grows Older
description: A poem from Morning in the Burned House (1995) in the voice of a calendar pin-up, Miss July, now grown old, who looks back on the body that was once her fortune.
plot_or_argument: Miss July - the girl on the July page of a nude calendar - speaks in the first person about her life since the photograph was taken. She remembers the body she had, and the power it gave her: 'I had a talent', she says in effect, and 'men were a skill'. She is unsentimental about her younger self, who was vain and not very intelligent, and unsentimental about the men who wanted her, whom she describes with a mixture of contempt and amusement. What has changed is not only her body but her relation to time: 'the way the sun moves through the hours becomes important', and the calendar has become a way of measuring what is left rather than what is on offer. The poem is neither a lament nor a joke. It gives the pin-up a mind and a voice, and lets her look steadily at the transaction she was once part of; by the end the reader is asked to see the ageing woman's self-knowledge as a form of power too, though a bleaker and lonelier one.
narrative_structure: A dramatic monologue in loose, short-lined free verse, without stanza divisions or an obvious rhyme scheme; the voice is colloquial and self-interrupting, and the poem moves by association from the calendar photograph to the young men, to the present body and to the passing of time.
meter_and_prosody: Conversational, ironic and deliberately flat in places, with sudden lyrical turns; short lines and abrupt enjambments; a diction that mixes the demotic ('Don't get me wrong') with precise physical and temporal notation; the tone is that of a woman talking to herself in a room.
historical_context: Morning in the Burned House (McClelland and Stewart, 1995) was Atwood's first collection of new poems for eight years and won the Trillium Award; its second section reworks female archetypes - Miss July, Helen of Troy and others - in monologues that draw on the feminist critique of the image and of the beauty myth developed in the 1970s and 1980s.
literary_significance: One of the best known poems of Morning in the Burned House and a frequently taught example of the feminist dramatic monologue; it is Atwood's selection in the Norton Anthology alongside 'Death by Landscape'.
bibliographical_notes: Published in Morning in the Burned House (Toronto: McClelland and Stewart, 1995; Boston: Houghton Mifflin, 1995). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 1043.
thematic_analysis: Atwood takes the most stereotyped of female images - the calendar girl, whose only function is to be looked at - and gives her the position of the speaking subject. The poem is a critique of the commerce in female beauty, but it refuses to absolve its speaker: Miss July enjoyed her power and used it, and the poem's honesty about that is what makes it more than a polemic. Ageing and the body's betrayal are the second subject, and the poem's final turn towards the sun and the hours makes mortality itself the measure of value.
summary: A dramatic monologue of some forty lines in which the ageing Miss July reflects on beauty, the calendar, the men who once looked at her, and the way the sun now moves through the hours.
research_notes: The poem was not read complete; the description follows the accounts in the Harvard Crimson review of the collection, the ProQuest article on the poem and the Oxford Research Encyclopedia chapter cited, which quote 'men were a skill' and 'the way the sun / moves through the hours becomes important'.

title: Waiting for the Barbarians
description: J. M. Coetzee's third novel (1980), the first-person testimony of an unnamed magistrate on a far frontier of an unnamed empire, who is broken by the state's security police for trying to return a tortured barbarian woman to her own people, and who learns in prison what the Empire's justice is.
plot_or_argument: The novel is narrated by the magistrate of a small settlement on the frontier of the Empire, a man who has spent his working life administering a place where nothing much happens, collecting antiquities and sleeping with a local woman. The Empire declares a state of emergency and sends the Third Bureau, its security service, under Colonel Joll, who interrogates and tortures a group of captives on suspicion of being barbarians. Joll leaves, the frontier empties, and the magistrate takes in a young barbarian woman left crippled and half-blind by the torture; he washes her feet, sleeps beside her, and cannot say what he wants from her. He decides to return her to her people and sets out with two soldiers and a horse across the salt flats, a journey the novel describes with a physical exactness that becomes an allegory of the Empire's ignorance of the land it claims. Having handed her over, he comes back to find the Third Bureau in charge and is arrested for desertion and for consorting with the enemy; he is imprisoned in a cellar, beaten, hung by the arms, and reduced to begging for food. When the imperial campaign collapses and Joll returns with captives for a public spectacle of torture, the magistrate interrupts it and is beaten again. The soldiers leave; the barbarians never appear. The novel ends with the magistrate helping the townspeople repair the walls and clean up, while the question of what the Empire was defending, and what the magistrate was complicit in, is left open.
narrative_structure: Six chronological chapters, narrated in the first person by the magistrate as a retrospective confession and testimony; the narrative is deliberately unadorned, with short scenes and summary rather than dramatised interiority, and the allegory depends on the suppression of names and historical particulars.
meter_and_prosody: A spare, grave, almost transparent prose; short declarative sentences and minimal metaphor; the lexicon of administration and bureaucracy (reports, warrants, requisitions, 'the Bureau'); first-person narration that reports physical detail with clinical precision and leaves moral judgment to the reader; dialogue in an unmarked, serviceable English.
historical_context: Waiting for the Barbarians was published by Secker and Warburg (London) on 27 October 1980, three years after In the Heart of the Country and before Life & Times of Michael K (1983); it won the James Tait Black Memorial Prize and the Geoffrey Faber Memorial Prize, takes its title and its central situation from Cavafy's poem 'Waiting for the Barbarians' (1904) and from Buzzati's The Tartar Steppe (1940), and was written in South Africa during the apartheid years and the border wars of the 1970s and 1980s.
literary_significance: The novel that established Coetzee's international reputation and one of the most widely taught allegories of colonial power in English; Philip Glass made an opera of it in 2005, it is central to the criticism of Coetzee's ethics, and it is his selection in the Norton Anthology, printed as the extract 'From Waiting for the Barbarians'.
bibliographical_notes: Published on 27 October 1980 by Secker and Warburg (London); 156 pages in the first hardcover edition. A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 1046; the Norton text is an extract, and this record covers the whole novel.
thematic_analysis: The novel is an allegory of empire and torture, but its resistances are deliberate: the Empire, the barbarians and even the town are unnamed, the frontier could be South Africa, Latin America or anywhere, and the magistrate's goodness is as compromised as the state's violence - he enjoys his authority, he is complicit in the settlement and he cannot undo what Joll does. Coetzee's subject is the way in which a decent official becomes part of a machine of cruelty and is then punished by that machine; the barbarian girl's body, which he wants to read as a text from which a meaning can be extracted, is the novel's image of the limits of interpretation. The Empire's enemy is finally its own invention, and the novel's ending - the barbarians do not come - makes the point that the threat was always a pretext.
summary: A novel in six parts: the magistrate's settled frontier town; the arrival of Colonel Joll and the Third Bureau; the magistrate's care for the blinded barbarian girl and his expedition to return her; his arrest, imprisonment and torture; the collapse of the imperial campaign; and his return, unbroken in his own mind but stripped, to the ordinary life of the town.
critical_context: The novel has been central to the critical literature on Coetzee and on the ethics of postcolonial representation: critics have read it against Cavafy's poem, against the South African border wars of the 1980s and against the philosophy of torture, and have debated whether allegory is a way of evading history or the only honest way of representing it. Its deliberate refusal of national names has been both praised as a universalising move and attacked as a withdrawal from specific South African responsibility; the recurrent reading of the magistrate as a version of the liberal conscience, complicit and self-deceived, has shaped the reception of all of Coetzee's later work, and the novel has been compared to Conrad's Heart of Darkness as a founding text of the colonial frontier narrative.
research_notes: The plot and publication details follow Wikipedia's article on the novel, read directly, which is consistent with the summary in Coetzee's article and with general accounts of the book; the novel was not read complete in this session.

title: Fond Memory
description: A poem from Boland's The Journey (1987) about her childhood in 1950s London, where an Irish girl at an English school learns that the songs she is taught are not, after all, her country.
plot_or_argument: Boland remembers a classroom in London, the children 'in darned worsted', the teacher, and a song sung from Thomas Moore's Irish Melodies - 'Oft in the Stilly Night', with its refrain about fond memory bringing 'the light of other days around me'. For the Irish child in an English school the song is both a link to home and an embarrassment: the other children sing it without knowing what they are singing, while she knows and cannot say. The poem's title takes the song's own phrase and turns it: 'fond memory' is what the emigrant lives on, but it is also the false consolation that makes a country into a song. The poem ends on the speaker's recognition that she thought this was her country - 'was, will be again' - and that the upward-straining music was a 'safe inventory of pain': a shared, sentimentalised account of Irish suffering that she was wrong to trust. The adult poem keeps the melody and withdraws the belief.
narrative_structure: Four irregular stanzas in free verse, with short lines and a syntax that breaks across line endings; the poem moves from scene (the classroom) to song (Moore's lyric) to reflection, and the final stanza's flat contradiction ('And I was wrong') turns the poem against itself.
meter_and_prosody: Plain, exact, conversational free verse with a deliberately unpoetic vocabulary and a few highly charged abstractions; the quoted song supplies the only regular rhythm, and the poem's own lines are broken to resist it; the tone is wry, wounded and self-correcting.
historical_context: The Journey (Carcanet, 1987) is the collection in which Boland turned from the inherited rhetoric of Irish poetry to her own history as a diplomat's daughter in London and New York; 'Fond Memory' and its companion 'An Irish Childhood in England: 1951' belong to that autobiographical turn, and 'Fond Memory' revises Thomas Moore's 'Oft in the Stilly Night' (Irish Melodies, 1808-1834).
literary_significance: One of Boland's most discussed poems of the 1980s and a set text in Irish schools; it is one of her three selections in the Norton Anthology and the poem most often used to introduce her treatment of exile and national identity.
bibliographical_notes: Published in The Journey and Other Poems (Manchester: Carcanet, 1987; New York: Carcanet, 1987). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 1059.
thematic_analysis: The poem is about the education of an emigrant child into a national identity she has not chosen and cannot quite own. Moore's melodies, which were the sound of Irish nationalism in middle-class drawing rooms on both sides of the Irish Sea, are shown to be a kind of manufactured memory, and the child's discomfort is the beginning of the poet's later critique of the rhetoric of Irish suffering. Displacement, class (the darned worsted, the London school) and the pressure of a national song on a private child run together, and the poem's irony is directed as much at the speaker's own longing as at the English school.
summary: A short poem in several unrhymed stanzas, recalling a London classroom, the teacher who taught the children Thomas Moore's Irish melodies, and the moment the child realised that the patriotism of the song did not belong to her.
research_notes: The poem was not read complete; the description follows the quotations and discussion in the Post Identity article on Boland and the Liverpool University Press chapter on her memory poems, both read as search extracts, which quote the closing lines and name Moore's song.

title: The Dolls Museum in Dublin
description: A poem from In a Time of Violence (1994) that walks through a Dublin museum of dolls and finds, behind the glass cases, Easter 1916 and the innocent society that the Rising destroyed.
plot_or_argument: The poem begins with the dolls' damage: 'The wounds are terrible. The paint is old', the cracks on the lips cannot be fixed, and the arms are 'ivory dissolved to wax'. From there the poem reconstructs the world the dolls belonged to - the Quadrille, the waltz, the yacht-club terraces, the carriage wheels on the cobbled quays - and then names the occasion: 'And recreate Easter in Dublin.' The second half is a sequence of images of the city in Easter week, 1916: booted officers and their mistresses, sunlight on College Green, the bar of the Shelbourne full, laughter on the terraces, rumour at the barracks, 'The Empire is summoning its officers' and the carriages turning back. Children walk with governesses, looking down at their dolls and then up at the passing carriage, 'the shadow chilling them'. The poem returns to the museum and to twilight: the shadows on the dolls are 'bruises on the stitched cotton clothes', and the dolls' wide eyes cannot address the helplessness of what they have survived. The last lines make them the keepers of a history they can record but not feel - 'To be the present of the past. / To infer the difference / with a terrible stare. / But not feel it. / And not know it.'
narrative_structure: Eleven unrhymed quatrains, mostly in loose iambic pentameter with occasional trimeter lines; the poem moves from description to reconstruction to reflection, and the last five short lines break the quatrain pattern to deliver the verdict on the dolls.
meter_and_prosody: Plain, declarative, almost flat in its diction, with a strong visual and tactile register (cracked paint, soiled cotton lawn, parchment-coloured waists); short sentences and a repeated imperative ('Recall... Hum... Promenade... Put back...') that makes the poem a guided tour; the rhythm is regular enough to feel like a museum catalogue and irregular enough to keep the reader uneasy.
historical_context: In a Time of Violence (Carcanet, 1994) is Boland's sequence of poems about Ireland, history and the violence of representation, including 'That the Science of Cartography Is Limited' and the title sequence; 'The Dolls Museum in Dublin' responds to the Easter Rising of 1916 and to the tradition of Yeats's poems on the Rising, and takes its title from the doll collection formerly displayed in Dublin.
literary_significance: One of the most anthologised Irish poems of the 1990s and a standard text for the study of Boland's historical poems; it is one of her three Norton selections and is widely read alongside Yeats's 'Easter 1916'.
bibliographical_notes: Published in In a Time of Violence (Manchester: Carcanet, 1994; New York: W. W. Norton, 1994). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 1060. The text is quoted here from the course page at Michigan State University, which prints the poem.
thematic_analysis: Boland reads the 1916 Rising through the objects of the society that it interrupted: the dolls are the possessions of the Anglo-Irish middle class whose world the Rising ended, and their damage is history's. The poem is an act of historical imagination that refuses nostalgia - the elegance of the Shelbourne and the yacht club is not defended, but the violence that ends it is not celebrated either - and its final insistence on the dolls' inability to feel or know is a warning about the museum as a way of remembering: glass cases preserve the past and drain it of consequence. The poem's ekphrastic gaze is also a feminist one, finding public history in the domestic and decorative objects of women and children.
summary: A poem in unrhymed quatrains that describes the dolls - their cracked paint, soiled cotton and waxen arms - and then reconstructs, through them, the Dublin of the Easter week of 1916, the officers, the terraces, the Shelbourne bar, and the children with their governesses on College Green.
research_notes: The poem's text was read complete on the Michigan State University course page, and the reading of it follows the discussion in the Post Identity article; the museum itself and the details of its collection were not otherwise verified.

title: The Lost Land
description: The title poem of Boland's 1998 collection: a woman with two grown daughters tries to give them a country, and finds that memory itself has become an emigrant.
plot_or_argument: The poem opens with an inventory of desire: 'I have two daughters. / They are all I ever wanted from the earth. / Or almost all.' What she wanted besides was 'one piece of ground', 'One city trapped by hills. One urban river. An island in its element', so that she could say 'mine. My own' and mean it. Now the daughters are grown and far away, and memory itself has become an emigrant, 'wandering in a place / where love dissembles itself as landscape', where the hills are the colours of a child's eyes and the children are 'distances, horizons'. At night, on the edge of sleep, she sees the shore of Dublin Bay and its granite pier and asks whether this is how the emigrants saw it, 'backing out on the mailboat at twilight'. The last movement imagines her own place at the landward rail of that boat, searching for the last sight of a hand, and then 'on the underworld side of that water' in the dark, saying over 'all the names I know for a lost land: / Ireland. Absence. Daughter.'
narrative_structure: Four movements of unequal length in free verse: the inventory of what she wanted, the emigration of memory, the imagined departure of the daughters, and the speaker's own imagined place on the boat; the poem ends with a three-word list that acts as a refrain and a summary.
meter_and_prosody: Short, spare lines and a conversational syntax; repetition ('One piece of ground', 'One city', 'One urban river') and anaphora; a plain vocabulary of landscape and family, with only a few charged metaphors ('memory itself / has become an emigrant'); the last lines are unpunctuated as a list.
historical_context: The Lost Land (Carcanet, 1998) is the collection in which Boland wrote most directly about emigration, the Famine and the Irish diaspora, and the title poem is its statement of theme; the 'underworld side of that water' draws on the classical descent to the dead as well as on the Irish emigrant's crossing, and the poem's Dublin Bay is the scene of the mailboat departures from Dún Laoghaire.
literary_significance: The title poem of one of Boland's central collections and among her most frequently quoted poems on emigration and motherhood; it is one of her three Norton selections.
bibliographical_notes: Published in The Lost Land (Manchester: Carcanet, 1998; New York: W. W. Norton, 1998). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 1061. The text is quoted here from the Poetry Foundation's printing.
thematic_analysis: The lost land of the title is not one place but three at once - Ireland, the past and the children - and the poem's power comes from refusing to separate them. Boland writes about emigration as a structure of feeling rather than an event: the mailboat, the railway pier and the dark water are the inherited images of Irish departure, and the poem's speaker finds herself, a woman who stayed, occupying the emigrant's position because her daughters have left. Motherhood and national belonging are placed on the same footing, and the poem's ending - the three names said in the dark - makes absence itself the ground on which identity is built.
summary: A short poem in free verse in which the speaker counts what she wanted from the earth - her daughters, and one piece of ground, one city, one river - and then imagines them leaving Ireland as generations had left it before.
research_notes: The poem's text was read complete on the Poetry Foundation page, which reports the 1998 Norton printing; the review in the January Magazine was also read as a search extract for the collection's reception.

title: The Glass Essay
description: Anne Carson's long poem from Glass, Irony and God (1995): a woman visits her mother in the country after a love affair ends, rereads Emily Brontë, and finds in Brontë's solitude and in the 'Nudes' she hallucinates an image of her own grief, in a poem that mixes lyric, narrative and literary criticism.
plot_or_argument: The poem begins with a journey: 'I travel all day on trains and bring a lot of books - / some for my mother, some for me / including The Collected Works of Emily Brontë. / This is my favourite author. / Also my main fear, which I mean to confront.' The speaker has come to visit her mother in the country after the end of an affair, and the flat, wintry landscape around her mother's house makes her feel she is turning into Emily Brontë - solitary, exposed, walking the moor, 'my ungainly body stumping over the mud flats'. The visit is ordinary and sad: the mother is brisk and unsentimental, the father is in a nursing home with Alzheimer's disease, and the speaker sleeps badly, wakes thinking of the man she calls Law, and sees in the mirror a face she hardly recognises. Throughout, she reads Brontë: the poems 'not at all like the poetry women generally write', the isolation of the Haworth parsonage, the death-haunted biography, and the accusation that Brontë's work is 'too much about the self'. Interleaved with this are the 'Nudes' - hallucinated figures of a woman, naked and exposed, that appear to her at the edge of sleep and grow more real and more compassionate as the poem goes on. The sections move between the mother's kitchen, the nursing home, the train, Brontë's letters and the snow-covered fields, and the poem ends without consolation, in a quiet acceptance that the self is not cured by reading or writing but is, for a moment, held.
narrative_structure: Nine numbered sections in a loose, long-lined free verse that often reads as prose; the sections shift between first-person narrative, close reading of Brontë's poems and of the 'Nudes', and disquisition on sound, hysteria and the gendering of emotion; the poem's continuity is thematic and imagistic rather than plotted, and its length (some thirty pages) makes it a verse essay.
meter_and_prosody: A style at once plain and strange: short declarative sentences, exact physical detail ('The April light is clear as an alarm'), and sudden abstract questions; the incorporation of quotation, footnote and scholarly aside; a deadpan humour (Aristotle's 'women are like things / that speak') set against passages of great tenderness; no regular metre or rhyme, but a strong rhythmic line shaped by breath and syntax.
historical_context: Glass, Irony and God was published by New Directions in 1995 and gathered 'The Glass Essay', 'Book of Isaiah' and 'The Fall of Rome'; Carson had already published Eros the Bittersweet (1986) and Plainwater (1995), and the poem's mixture of classics, autobiography and literary criticism became the model for much of her later work. Its Brontë material belongs to the feminist rereading of the nineteenth-century woman writer, and its form to the tradition of the long poem as essay that runs from the Romantics through to the twentieth century.
literary_significance: The poem that established Carson's reputation with a general readership and the most widely discussed of her works; it is her selection in the Norton Anthology, printed as an extract, and it is a standard text in courses on the long poem, on the essay and on contemporary Canadian poetry.
bibliographical_notes: Published in Glass, Irony and God (New York: New Directions, 1995). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 1075; the Norton text is an extract, and this record covers the whole poem.
thematic_analysis: The poem's subject is grief that has no socially sanctioned form - the grief of a woman abandoned by a lover, which the poem examines with the same seriousness as death - and it puts that grief beside Brontë's, whose loneliness is both a literary inheritance and a warning. Carson refuses the confessional bargain of the 'sincere' poem: 'The Glass Essay' quotes, translates, annotates and essayises, and its intellectual work is part of its feeling, not a retreat from it. The mother-daughter relation, the failing father and the 'three silent women at the kitchen table' - mother, daughter and Brontë - make a counter-family of women whose intimacy is partly made of reading, and the Nudes, which begin as images of exposure, become a way of imagining a female suffering that is not shameful and not alone.
summary: A sequence of nine numbered sections, mixing lyric, narrative and essay, in which the speaker travels to her mother's house, reads Emily Brontë's poems and Wuthering Heights, describes the 'Nudes' that appear to her in bed and on the road, and considers the end of a love affair and the decline of her father.
critical_context: Criticism has treated 'The Glass Essay' as the defining example of Carson's mixed-genre poetics: readings of the poem have concentrated on its use of Brontë as a double, on the 'Nudes' as figures for the female body in pain, and on the essay form as a way of thinking through feeling. The poem is central to the critical case for Carson as a poet who has renewed the long poem, and it is frequently compared with her later verse novels and with the confessional tradition she is said to have revised rather than continued; its account of reading as consolation and of consolation's limits has been influential in discussions of literature and grief.
research_notes: The text was read in substantial part through the quotations in the reviews and study material cited and through the opening passages reproduced in them; the poem was not read complete. The accounts of the nine sections, the Nudes and the poem's ending follow those sources and general knowledge.

title: Anseo
description: A poem from Why Brownlee Left (1980) about a school roll call in Irish - 'Anseo', here - and the schoolboy, Joseph Mary Plunkett Ward, who learns obedience in the classroom and later commands an IRA unit.
plot_or_argument: The poem opens with the word itself: 'Anseo' is the first word of Irish the speaker learned, 'the first word of Irish I spoke', and it means 'here, here and now, / All present and correct'. The scene is a classroom in a Catholic school in the north, where the master, with 'an ash-plant, a salley-rod', calls the roll in Irish and the boys must answer. Joseph Mary Plunkett Ward is the boy who does not answer, who is late, who is beaten; the poem follows him through the school's regime of punishment - the master's 'careful' violence, the naming of the boys after Irish patriots - until he leaves. The last stanza jumps forward: Ward, now 'Joe Ward', the diminutive marking his change, is a commandant of an IRA unit, and 'His volunteers would call back Anseo / And raise their hands / As their names occurred.' The poem does not comment. It shows a single word carrying both the intimacy of a language and the discipline of an army, and leaves the reader to see how the schoolroom's obedience became the paramilitary's.
narrative_structure: A short narrative in unrhymed quatrains and longer stanzas, moving chronologically from the roll call to the beating to the leap forward to Ward's command; the last stanza repeats the answering word and gesture of the first, closing the poem on a rhyme of institutions.
meter_and_prosody: Spare, exact, colloquial verse with a strong iambic pulse, short lines and abrupt enjambment; a mixture of Irish words, Northern Irish speech ('He would arrive as a matter of course') and literary naming; almost no metaphor, and no overt comment; a tone of dry, withheld irony.
historical_context: Why Brownlee Left (Faber, 1980) was Muldoon's third collection and the one in which the Troubles and his County Armagh childhood became explicit subjects; 'Anseo' is one of a group of poems about school, family and the inheritance of Irish nationalism, and its Irish-language title belongs to the period's debate over language and identity in the north.
literary_significance: One of Muldoon's most anthologised and most taught poems, a standard text on the Troubles and on the politics of language in Northern Irish poetry; it is his first selection in the Norton Anthology.
bibliographical_notes: Published in Why Brownlee Left (London: Faber and Faber, 1980). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 1080.
thematic_analysis: The poem is about the Irish language as a shibboleth and as an instrument of authority: 'Anseo' is the word of presence and of being accounted for, and Muldoon lets it pass from the roll call of a primary school to the roll call of an IRA unit without a break. Education, punishment and nationalist inheritance are shown as a single system, and the poem's irony is directed at the schooling that produced soldiers - the boys named after the executed leaders of 1916 become the volunteers of the 1970s. The Norther Ireland of the Troubles is present only at the edges, in the name of the master, the ash-plant and the final roll call, and the poem's restraint is part of its judgement.
summary: A short narrative poem in several unrhymed stanzas: the master calls the roll, the boys answer 'Anseo', and one of them, Ward, is beaten into answering and later answers to a different name and a different kind of roll call.
research_notes: The poem was not read complete; the account follows the quotations and discussion in the Brill chapter on Why Brownlee Left, the Galway poem database entries, the Slate review of the Selected Poems and general knowledge, which agree on the roll call, Ward's name and the IRA ending.

title: Meeting the British
description: The title poem of Muldoon's 1987 collection: an eighteenth-century Native American speaker recalls the winter meeting with General Amherst and Colonel Bouquet, who gave his people six fishhooks and two blankets embroidered with smallpox.
plot_or_argument: 'We met the British in the dead of winter.' The speaker, a Native American, describes the meeting in a forest clearing: the sky lavender, the snow lavender-blue, two frozen streams coming together, and the strangeness of hearing himself 'calling out in French across that forest-clearing'. General Jeffrey Amherst and Colonel Henry Bouquet cannot stomach the people's willow-tobacco; the Colonel shakes out a handkerchief and explains, in French, that the scent is lavender, 'une fleur mauve comme le ciel'. The poem ends with the transaction: 'They gave us six fishhooks / and two blankets embroidered with smallpox.' Nothing follows: no reaction, no death, no reflection. The withheld last word is the poem's whole meaning, and the courteous, scented, lavender-coloured scene is revealed as the setting of a deliberate act of biological warfare.
narrative_structure: A single eighteen-line stanza of short lines without stanza breaks; the poem proceeds as a first-person anecdote in the past tense, with two lines of quoted French, and closes on a single sentence that delivers the poem's withheld information.
meter_and_prosody: Flat, understated, almost prosaic free verse with a strong stress pulse; exact colour words (lavender, mauve) and precise physical detail (frozen streams, fishhooks, embroidered blankets); the juxtaposition of French quotation and English reportage; no metaphor except the terrible one of the embroidery.
historical_context: Meeting the British (Faber, 1987) was Muldoon's fifth collection, published in the year he moved to the United States; the title poem draws on the documented distribution of smallpox-contaminated blankets to Delaware delegates at Fort Pitt in 1763, during Pontiac's War, and belongs to the 1980s Irish debate about colonialism, the north and the uses of history.
literary_significance: One of Muldoon's best known and most frequently anthologised poems, a standard text in postcolonial criticism of Irish poetry; it is one of his selections in the Norton Anthology and gives its title to the collection.
bibliographical_notes: Published in Meeting the British (London: Faber and Faber, 1987). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 1081.
thematic_analysis: The poem dramatises the colonial encounter as a failed and fatal act of communication: the speaker's French, the Colonel's French, the lavender and the smallpox all belong to a vocabulary the Native Americans are given but cannot control. Muldoon's subject is the 'gift' as an instrument of empire, and the poem's historical reference - the blankets distributed at Fort Pitt during Pontiac's War in 1763 - makes it an indictment of British colonial practice that Irish readers have always read as an analogy for their own history. The poem's brevity and its refusal of lament are the source of its anger: the atrocity is delivered as a courtesy, in the tone of a travel anecdote.
summary: An eighteen-line poem in a single stanza, spoken by a Native American who describes a meeting with two British officers in a forest clearing, the exchange of willow-tobacco and scented handkerchief, and the gifts that carry disease.
research_notes: The poem's text was read complete through the reproduction in the Tumblr poetry post and the analysis pages cited, which agree word for word; the historical background follows the Encyclopedia.com guide and the accounts of the Fort Pitt incident in the sources cited.

title: 7, Middagh Street
description: A long sequence at the end of Meeting the British (1987) in which seven people who lived or visited the house at 7 Middagh Street, Brooklyn Heights, in 1940-41 - Auden, Gypsy Rose Lee, Britten, Kallman, Dalí, McCullers and MacNeice - speak in turn.
plot_or_argument: The poem is set in a rented house in Brooklyn Heights where, in 1940-41, W. H. Auden, the burlesque dancer Gypsy Rose Lee, the composer Benjamin Britten, Auden's lover Chester Kallman, the painter Salvador Dalí, the novelist Carson McCullers and the poet Louis MacNeice lodged or visited. Each of the seven speaks in turn, and Muldoon writes each in a form suited to the voice: Auden in tetrameters and syllabics, lectures and catechisms; Gypsy Rose Lee in the language of the stage; Britten in letters and musical notation; Dalí in outrageous aphorisms; McCullers in a prose that echoes her own fiction; MacNeice in lyric stanzas and in his diaries' idiom. Across the sequence the talk is of art and its uses, of the war in Europe and the United States' non-intervention, of sex and of money. The poem's frame is the question of what a community of artists is for: the house is a 'February House', a temporary gathering of people with nothing in common but their work, and Muldoon lets each speak his or her own prejudices and self-deceptions. The sequence ends with MacNeice, the poet closest to Muldoon in background and trade, and with a movement out of the house and into the war.
narrative_structure: A sequence of seven monologues, each in a different form and voice, with a prologue and interconnecting passages; the poem is one of Muldoon's longest and most architecturally organised, using section numbers, changing line lengths and typography to distinguish voices, and closing with MacNeice's section as a coda.
meter_and_prosody: A polyphonic poem whose style changes with each speaker; Auden's section is metrical, didactic and colloquial, Gypsy Rose Lee's is theatrical and punning, McCullers's is lyrical and gothic, MacNeice's is plain, wry and occasional; throughout, Muldoon's own wordplay and rhymes surface in every voice.
historical_context: Meeting the British (Faber, 1987) ends with '7, Middagh Street', written after Muldoon had moved from Belfast to Cambridge and then to the United States; the house at 7 Middagh Street was the 'February House' described in Sherill Tippins's book of that name, and the poem draws on Auden's and MacNeice's correspondence and on the history of the period 1940-41, when Britain stood alone and the United States was not yet at war.
literary_significance: Muldoon's most ambitious long poem of the 1980s and the one that established his interest in the sequence and in the ventriloquism of historical voices; it is one of his selections in the Norton Anthology, printed as an extract, and a standard point of reference in criticism of his politics and poetics.
bibliographical_notes: Published in Meeting the British (London: Faber and Faber, 1987); the sequence runs to some twenty pages in Poems 1968-1998 (Faber, 2001), pp. 175-193. A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 1082, where it is printed with the opening line '(And were Yeats living at this hour)'; the Norton text is an extract, and this record covers the whole sequence.
thematic_analysis: The poem is a study of the relation between art and politics: the artists in the house are famous, self-absorbed and mostly wrong about the war and about themselves, and Muldoon's ventriloquism lets their voices be brilliant and unreliable at once. The house at 7 Middagh Street is an image of modernism in exile, a community of gay and eccentric artists in wartime Brooklyn, and the sequence's interest in money, sex and reputation is a corrective to the idea of modernist purity. The Irish strand (MacNeice and, through him, Muldoon's own Northern Irish inheritance) makes the poem a meditation on what a poet from a small country does with the great moderns.
summary: A sequence of some twenty pages of monologues in different metres and forms, spoken by the seven inhabitants of the Brooklyn house in the winter of 1940-41, about art, politics, sex and the war in Europe.
research_notes: The sequence was not read complete; the account follows the Brill chapter on Meeting the British, the Galway poem database entry, the Boston Globe account of February House and the Guardian essay by Giles Foden, which agree on the seven speakers, the house and the poem's concerns.

title: Milkweed and Monarch
description: A villanelle from The Annals of Chile (1994) in which the poet kneels at his parents' grave and finds his mouth filled not with grief for them but with the taste of a former lover's pickled gherkin.
plot_or_argument: 'As he knelt by the grave of his mother and father / the taste of dill, or tarragon - / he could barely tell one from the other - / filled his mouth.' The poem's opening moves from the grave to the palate, and its confusion of the two parents is also a confusion of places and times: the graveyard at Collegelands, the herbs of an Irish childhood, the American sea otter and the 'pickled gherkin' of a girlfriend in the United States, the Cliffs of Moher and a Russian samovar. The refrains turn on the doubles of the title - milkweed and monarch, the plant and the butterfly that feeds on it, inseparable and mutually dependent - and on the speaker's inability to 'tell one from the other'. The poem's central grief is displaced: the dead parents are half-forgotten in the surge of erotic memory, and the mother's name ('Regan') is misread as 'Anger', which is the poem's admission of what it feels. The last tercets return to the grave, and the quatrain closes on the doubled refrain, so that the elegy ends in the state of not being able to distinguish, which the poem has made its form.
narrative_structure: A villanelle in twenty-five lines: seven tercets and a closing quatrain, with two refrains that alternate and recur; the poem's syntax runs across the stanza breaks, and the rhymes are half-rhymes and assonantal chimes rather than full rhymes, so that the form is both strict and unsettled.
meter_and_prosody: Highly wrought, punning verse with a strong rhyme-drive and a diction that mixes the literary (Moher, samovar) with the domestic (gherkin, dill, tarragon); short lines, heavy enjambment and internal echoes; a tone of dry, wounded irony that breaks into tenderness at the refrains.
historical_context: The Annals of Chile (Faber, 1994) won the T. S. Eliot Prize and contains 'Incantata', the elegy for the artist Mary Farl Powers, and 'Yarrow', as well as 'Milkweed and Monarch', written after the deaths of Muldoon's mother (1974) and father (1985); the poem's graveyard is at Collegelands, near The Moy, and its American material belongs to the years Muldoon spent teaching in the United States from 1987.
literary_significance: One of the most admired short poems of Muldoon's middle period and a frequently anthologised modern villanelle; it is one of his selections in the Norton Anthology and the poem through which his use of fixed forms is usually introduced.
bibliographical_notes: Published in The Annals of Chile (London: Faber and Faber, 1994). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 1083.
thematic_analysis: The poem is about the way grief is contaminated by other feelings: the speaker cannot mourn his parents without the intrusion of a lover, and cannot think of the lover without the parents' grave. Muldoon uses the villanelle's two refrains as the vehicle of that doubleness, so that the form itself performs the confusion of identities, and the poem's wit - 'savour', 'palaver', 'Moher', 'samovar' - is not decoration but the mind's attempt to keep moving. The poem is also an elegy for a marriage and for a childhood landscape, and its refusal of decorum (anger, erotic memory and food at the graveside) is a deliberate breach of the conventions of the elegy.
summary: A twenty-five-line poem in seven tercets and a quatrain, built on two refrains, in which a visit to the grave of the speaker's mother and father gives way to memories of a woman and of the plants and foods of childhood.
research_notes: The poem's opening and several lines were read through the quotations in the Brill chapter, The Independent's review of The Annals of Chile and the study pages cited, which agree on the villanelle form, the refrains and the poem's occasion; it was not read complete.

title: First Screening
description: A suite of twelve kinetic poems that bpNichol programmed in Apple BASIC on an Apple IIe in 1983-84 and issued through Underwhich Editions on a 5.25-inch floppy disk: an early and influential work of electronic literature.
plot_or_argument: First Screening was made in 1983 and 1984, when Nichol taught himself enough Apple BASIC to program the Apple IIe. The suite consists of twelve poems, each a short program: in one, a letter travels across the screen and returns; in another, words fall apart into their letters and reassemble; in another, a line of text scrolls and loops. The poems have no printed page. Their unit is the screen and the cycle of the loop, and their meaning is inseparable from the movement: a word that dissolves as you watch it cannot be read the way a printed word is read. 'Off-Screen Romance', one of the best known of the twelve, sends words across the screen like dancers. Nichol issued the suite through Underwhich Editions as 100 numbered and signed copies on 5.25-inch disks with printed matter, and it soon became inaccessible as the Apple IIe and then the HyperCard platform died; it was recreated in HyperCard by J. B. Hohm in 1992 and in JavaScript by Jim Andrews and others in 2007, and those recreations are now the usual way the work is read.
narrative_structure: Twelve separate short programs, each a self-contained poem, presented in sequence on a floppy disk; each runs as a loop, so the poem has no fixed beginning or end, and the suite as a whole is organised as a set of variations on movement and transformation rather than as a narrative.
meter_and_prosody: Programmed kinetic typography: capital and lower-case letters, words and short phrases moved by BASIC commands; simple line-drawn shapes and colour changes; repetition, looping and delay as rhythmic devices; the aesthetic is that of the typewriter poem and the animated cartoon at once.
historical_context: Nichol made First Screening after two decades of typewriter and concrete poetry, and issued it through Underwhich Editions, the imprint he had founded in 1979; it belongs to the first wave of literary works made for the personal computer, alongside the experiments of the 1980s in hypertext and computer animation, and it has become a founding example in the historiography of electronic literature.
literary_significance: One of the earliest works of programmed kinetic poetry in English and the work through which Nichol is known in the field of electronic literature; its selection in the Norton Anthology is a landmark in the anthologising of digital writing, and its reconstruction history is a standard case study in the preservation of born-digital art.
bibliographical_notes: Programmed in Apple BASIC on the Apple IIe in 1983-84 and issued by Underwhich Editions (Toronto, 1984) as 100 numbered and signed copies on 5.25-inch floppy disks with printed matter. Recreated in HyperCard by J. B. Hohm (1992) and in JavaScript by Jim Andrews, Geof Huth, Lionel Kearns, Marko Niemi and Dan Waber (2007). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, at page 1117.
thematic_analysis: First Screening continues Nichol's concrete-poetry concern with the letter as a visual and material object, but it adds time: the poem is a sequence of positions and transformations rather than a static arrangement, and the reader's attention is held by the movement rather than the page. The suite's subject is the instability of language - words that will not stay put, letters that lose their place - and, implicitly, the new medium's own fragility: the work was made obsolete within a decade of its making, and its history is now part of what it is about.
summary: Twelve short programmed poems in which letters and words move, mutate, dissolve and re-form on the screen; distributed as a signed floppy disk with printed matter, later recreated in HyperCard and JavaScript.
research_notes: The work was not run in its original form. The account follows the Rhizome editorial on the 2007 reconstruction, which reproduces the history of the Underwhich edition, and the Wikipedia article on bpNichol; the descriptions of individual poems are limited to those named in those sources.

title: My Son the Fanatic
description: A story first published in 1994 and collected in Love in a Blue Time (1997): Parvez, a Pakistani taxi driver in an English city, watches his son Ali reject his parents' assimilated life for a strict Islam, and cannot understand what has happened to him.
plot_or_argument: Parvez, a Pakistani immigrant who has driven a taxi in an unnamed English city for more than twenty years, notices that his son Ali is behaving strangely: he has stopped eating with the family, given up his accounting studies for prayer, thrown away his tapes and clothes, and grown a beard. Fearing drugs, Parvez searches Ali's room and finds a prayer mat and a Quran. He consults his two closest friends, who advise him that the boy must be on drugs, and Bettina, a prostitute he drives regularly, who tells him to look in the boy's room and then, later, to talk to him. Parvez takes Ali to a restaurant, where he drinks too much and Ali lectures him on the filth of the West, on his drinking and on his friendship with a prostitute. When Bettina later tries to talk to Ali in the taxi, Ali insults her and she leaves. The story ends with Parvez, drunk and enraged, going into his son's room and beating him, while Ali neither defends himself nor retaliates; the last words of the story are Ali's: 'So who's the fanatic now?'
narrative_structure: A short story in a series of short scenes, told in the third person from Parvez's point of view, moving between the taxi, the family house, his friends' shop and the restaurant; the story's dialogue carries most of the action, and its ending with Ali's question is a deliberate reversal of the title.
meter_and_prosody: Colloquial, fast-moving prose with a strong ear for the speech of the taxi trade and the immigrant household; free indirect style used to render Parvez's puzzlement; comedy of embarrassment and misunderstanding; short paragraphs and abrupt cuts, as in a screenplay.
historical_context: The story was first published in 1994 and collected in Love in a Blue Time (Faber, 1997), Kureishi's first collection of stories; it belongs to the British Asian writing of the 1990s and to the decade's debate about Islam, race and multiculturalism in Britain, and was filmed by Udayan Prasad in 1997 with Om Puri and Rachel Griffiths.
literary_significance: One of Kureishi's most widely taught stories and a set text in British schools on identity and multiculturalism; it is his selection in the Norton Anthology and the story most often used to introduce his fiction.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1994 and collected in Love in a Blue Time (London: Faber and Faber, 1997). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 1151.
thematic_analysis: The story is about the failure of a father's model of assimilation: Parvez has worked to become English, and his son's religion exposes the bargain as a loss. Kureishi refuses to make either position simply right: Ali's Islam is shown as rigid and intolerant, but the West Parvez defends is one of drinking, prostitutes and the money that pays for both, and the story's sympathy is with the father's bewilderment rather than his values. The conflict between generations, between secular and religious authority, and between an immigrant's public performance of belonging and his private life is played out in domestic scenes, and the ending - violence answered by a question - leaves the moral judgement unresolved.
summary: A short story in six or seven scenes, in which Parvez investigates his son's change of life, consults his friends and a prostitute named Bettina, takes Ali to dinner, and finally confronts him with violence.
research_notes: The plot follows the paraphrase on the Wikipedia article and the several summaries read as search extracts, which agree on Parvez, Ali, Bettina and the closing question; the story was not read complete, and the first publication year and the collection date are those given in those sources.

title: Warming Her Pearls
description: A poem from Selling Manhattan (1987) spoken by a maid who is made to wear her mistress's pearl necklace against her skin all day, to warm it, and whose service becomes an unspoken and unreturned desire.
plot_or_argument: 'Next to my own skin, her pearls.' The maid speaks: her mistress bids her wear the pearls and warm them until evening, when she will brush her hair and fasten them round her 'cool, white throat'. All day she thinks of her mistress in the Yellow Room, choosing between silk and taffeta, fanning herself, while the maid works 'willingly, my slow heat entering / each pearl'. The necklace is 'slack on my neck, her rope' - an image of both intimacy and servitude. In the attic at night she dreams of her, pictures her dancing with tall men, and feels the pearls' absence cooling in the room below: 'All night / I feel their absence and I burn.' The poem never names the desire as lesbian or as hopeless; it is carried entirely by the pearls, which pass between the two women's bodies and hold the maid's heat against the mistress's skin. The class relation is inseparable from the erotic one: the mistress's beauty is the product of the maid's labour, and the intimacy the maid is allowed is the intimacy of service.
