narrative_structure: Six quatrains in loose iambic pentameter, unrhymed but heavily alliterative and assonantal; the poem moves through a single day and night, from the morning putting-on of the pearls to the night-time absence, and ends on a one-line sentence that breaks the stanza's flow.
meter_and_prosody: Restrained, sensuous, cool in diction and hot in implication; long vowel sounds and soft consonants; domestic detail used as erotic notation (skin, throat, hair, heat); the tone is that of a servant's even and uncomplaining report, which makes the last line's 'I burn' a shock.
historical_context: Selling Manhattan (Anvil Press, 1987) was Duffy's second major collection and won the Somerset Maugham Award; the poem draws on the historical practice of warming pearls against the skin to improve their lustre, and belongs to the 1980s revival of the dramatic monologue and to the lesbian and feminist poetry of the period.
literary_significance: One of the most anthologised poems of Duffy's early career and a standard text on desire, class and the dramatic monologue in modern British poetry; it is her first selection in the Norton Anthology.
bibliographical_notes: Published in Selling Manhattan (London: Anvil Press Poetry, 1987). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning on page 1159.
thematic_analysis: The poem is about desire that can only be expressed as work: the maid's body heats the pearls that will decorate another woman's body, and her feeling is transferred along with her warmth. Duffy makes the Victorian and Edwardian household - the Yellow Room, the toilette, the attic - the setting for a study of class and sexuality together, so that the power that keeps the maid in service is the same power that makes her desire unspeakable. The pearls are a fetish in the precise sense: an object that stands for a body and carries its heat, and the poem's final burn is both sexual frustration and the physical resentment of a servant.
summary: A dramatic monologue in six quatrains in which the maid describes the daily ritual of the pearls, the mistress's toilette, her own attic bed and her sleepless nights, and admits at last that she burns.
research_notes: The poem was read complete in the text reproduced on the Poem Analysis page; the reading of the class and desire material follows that page and general criticism, and the historical note on warming pearls is that page's account, not verified elsewhere.

title: Valentine
description: A poem from Mean Time (1993) that offers an onion instead of a rose or a satin heart, and uses it to say what love is actually like: layered, tear-making, possessive and lasting.
plot_or_argument: The poem opens by refusing the conventional Valentine - 'Not a red rose or a satin heart' - and offers the onion instead: 'It is a moon wrapped in brown paper. / It promises light / like the careful undressing of love.' The onion will make the lover cry, as love does, and will turn her reflection into 'a wobbling photo of grief'. The speaker insists on it - 'I am trying to be truthful' - and rejects the commercial tokens, 'a cute card or a kissogram'. Then the poem's second half darkens: the onion's 'fierce kiss' will stay on the lips, its 'platinum loops' can shrink to a wedding ring 'if you like', and it is 'Lethal'. It will cling to the fingers, to the knife, for weeks - the smell of it a warning of possessiveness, of the knife that could be used. The poem ends with the onion's after-scent persisting, the gift accepted and the danger named at once.
narrative_structure: Free verse in irregular stanzas of one to six lines, with no rhyme scheme; the poem is built on the repetition of 'I give you an onion' and on a series of short, end-stopped sentences; the single-word lines ('Here.', 'Lethal.') act as beats of emphasis.
meter_and_prosody: Plain, monosyllabic, spoken diction with sharp, concrete images (moon wrapped in brown paper, platinum loops, knife); the conceit sustained with logical rigour; a tone that moves from playful refusal to sensual tenderness to flat menace without changing register.
historical_context: Mean Time (Anvil Press, 1993) won the Whitbread Poetry Award and contains many of Duffy's best known love poems; 'Valentine' belongs to the early 1990s vogue for the anti-romantic love poem and to Duffy's project of writing in the plain speech of the demotic, and it has become one of the most widely set poems in British schools.
literary_significance: The most famous poem of Duffy's middle period and one of the most widely taught poems in Britain; it is her selection in the Norton Anthology alongside 'Warming Her Pearls', 'Medusa' and 'Mrs Lazarus', and it is the poem through which her use of the conceit is usually introduced.
bibliographical_notes: Published in Mean Time (London: Anvil Press Poetry, 1993). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning at page 1160.
thematic_analysis: Duffy's subject is the honesty that the conventional language of romance prevents: the onion is a better emblem of love than the rose because it has layers, makes you cry, leaves a smell and cannot be disposed of quickly. The poem plays the metaphysical conceit - an ordinary object made to carry an argument about love - against the debased currency of the Valentine's card, and its final movement from tenderness to threat ('Lethal', the knife) refuses the separation of love from possession and violence. The 'if you like' of the wedding ring makes the marriage proposal a question the lover can decline, and the whole poem is addressed to a 'you' whose answer is not recorded.
summary: A short poem in irregular free-verse stanzas, in which the speaker gives her lover an onion, compares it to the moon wrapped in brown paper, to tears and to a wedding ring, and warns that its scent will cling to the knife.
research_notes: The poem was read in the quotations reproduced on the revision and study pages cited, which agree word for word on the opening, the moon and brown paper, 'Lethal' and the knife; it was not read complete from the printed collection.
